samples.text:
In many cities around the world, the government has put a lot of security cameras in public places like streets, stations and shopping centres. The aim is to reduce crime. In my opinion, this has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that cameras can stop people from committing crimes. If a thief knows that a camera is watching him, he will probably not steal anything because he is afraid to be caught. So the streets become safer. Secondly, when a crime happens, the police can watch the video and find the criminal more quickly. The recordings can also be used as evidence in court. Moreover, people feel more safe when they walk at night in areas with cameras, especially women and old people.

However, there are also some disadvantages. The most important one is privacy. Many people do not like that they are watched all the time when they are in public. They feel like the government is controlling them. Also, the information from cameras can be used in a wrong way, for example if someone share the videos on the internet. Another disadvantage is the cost. Installing and checking thousands of cameras is very expensive, and some people think that the money should spent on more police officers. In addition, criminals can simply move to other areas where there is not cameras.

In conclusion, security cameras have some problems such as privacy and cost. But I believe they help to reduce crime and make people feel safe, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. However, the government must make rules about how the videos are used.
samples.why: Clear position and judgement · relevant ideas on both sides but mostly listed rather than developed · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · comparative, agreement and passive errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In an effort to fight crime, many cities have installed extensive networks of surveillance cameras in streets, transport hubs and other public spaces. While this raises concerns about privacy and cost, I believe the advantages are greater.

The most important benefit of CCTV is its role in solving crimes. When an offence takes place in a monitored area, footage can help the police to identify suspects, trace their movements and provide strong evidence in court. This increases the chance that offenders are caught and punished, which in turn may discourage others. Cameras can also act as a deterrent in themselves; people planning to commit theft or vandalism are likely to think twice if they know they are being recorded. In addition, surveillance can help authorities respond quickly to emergencies, such as accidents or fights in crowded places, and it gives many members of the public a greater sense of security, particularly at night.

On the other hand, there are some drawbacks. The most frequently mentioned is the loss of privacy, as ordinary citizens are recorded constantly while going about their daily lives. There is a risk that footage could be misused, for example to monitor peaceful protesters or be leaked online. Critics also argue that cameras do not really reduce crime but simply move it to areas without surveillance. Finally, installing and monitoring thousands of cameras requires a considerable amount of public money that could be spent on other services.

Despite these concerns, I would argue that the problems can be managed through clear laws on who can access footage and how long it is kept.

In conclusion, although security cameras raise legitimate questions about privacy and value for money, their contribution to detecting and preventing crime makes them a worthwhile tool. Therefore, the advantages outweighs the disadvantages, as long as their use is properly regulated.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported, counter-arguments acknowledged · logical organisation · good collocation (act as a deterrent, value for money) · frequent error-free sentences, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Surveillance cameras have become a familiar feature of streets, stations and squares in many cities, justified primarily as a means of reducing crime. Although their spread raises serious questions about privacy and civil liberties, I believe that, under proper regulation, their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

The strongest argument for public CCTV lies in its investigative value. Footage can establish a clear sequence of events, identify suspects and corroborate or challenge witness statements, often transforming cases that would otherwise remain unsolved. This is particularly important for crimes such as street robbery, where victims may have only a fleeting glimpse of the offender. Cameras may also exert a deterrent effect, especially in car parks and transport hubs, where opportunistic offences are common. Beyond crime, surveillance systems allow authorities to manage crowds at large events, locate missing people and coordinate rapid responses to accidents.

The disadvantages, nonetheless, deserve careful consideration. Blanket surveillance changes the nature of public space: people who know they are constantly observed may feel less free to gather, protest or simply behave spontaneously. The potential for misuse is considerable, whether through unauthorised access, the leaking of footage or, more worryingly, the combination of cameras with facial recognition to track individuals without their knowledge. Critics also point out that cameras are less effective against impulsive crime than their supporters claim, and that some offending is merely displaced to unmonitored streets, which raises doubts about whether the substantial public expenditure is justified.

These risks, however, point to the need for firm safeguards rather than the removal of cameras altogether. Strict limits on data retention, independent oversight and transparent rules on facial recognition can preserve most of the benefits while protecting civil liberties.

In conclusion, security cameras are not a complete solution to crime, and their misuse could threaten personal freedom. Nevertheless, their value in solving and deterring offences means that, carefully regulated, their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.
samples.why: Sufficiently addresses both sides with a clear, qualified judgement · ideas logically sequenced and fully extended · cohesion managed skilfully · wide, precise vocabulary (corroborate, displaced, oversight) · wide range of error-free structures.
